FY23 Results Electro-polishing AM metals have the potential to exhibit high strength retention, but surface roughness can significantly impact fatigue performance. The layer-by-layer fusion process inherent to L-PBF can result in rough surfaces, characterized by partially melted particles and laser track lines. To fully understand the impact of these surface roughness features on mechanical performance, it is essential to investigate the effects of surface finishing after additive manufacturing. While various surface finishing techniques are available, physical-based methods are often limited to simple, line-of-sight paths, which can be a constraint when working with complex shapes. Additive manufacturing offers the unique advantage of creating complex geometries with relative ease. Chemical and electrochemical methods, such as electrochemical surface finishing, are being explored as effective ways to polish materials across complex shapes. Electrochemical polishing, in particular, offers the distinct advantage of tunable surface feature targeting through input signal control. By applying an electrical bias across two electrodes in an electrolyte solution, electrochemical reactions are catalyzed, enabling the selective removal of material from "high points" and resulting in a polished surface. In this study, electropolishing was tested using a commercial electropolishing solution (EPS 2500) and a home-made salt electrolyte, comprised of water, salt, and polyethylene glycol (PEG). The PEG electrolyte, initially optimized for 316L stainless steel, was verified to be effective for 316H stainless steel as well. A pulse waveform was developed to target partially melted particles using the PEG electrolyte, making surfaces more uniform and minimizing material loss. A 2-step electropolishing procedure was employed, involving the PEG electrolyte UNCLASSIFIED AMMT – 316H SS Los Alamos National Laboratory Page 3-19 to remove partially melted particles, followed by polishing in the commercial solution to rapidly target mesoscale waviness and homogenize the surface chemistry. To validate the polishing process, initial rectangular coupons of varied build angles were tested, followed by the polishing of cylindrical samples representative of tensile bars. Schema Step 1 Step 2 1 PEG-400, H2O, NaCl, NaNO3 – 200s EPS 2500 – 100s 2 PEG-400, H2O, NaCl, NaNO3 – 200s EPS 2500 – 1000s After careful consideration, schema 2 was selected for the provided samples, as it was found to be more effective in removing surface fatigue sites (as discussed below). Two electropolished 316H stainless steel samples were prepared for tensile testing. The surface characterization was conducted using a Keyence VK-3000 optical profilometer, with background subtraction applied prior to measuring the arithmetic mean height (Sa). An area of 2.5 μm by 2.5 μm was collected for each sample before and after polishing to assess surface roughness and uniformity. The polishing process was optimized to minimize roughness while simultaneously minimizing material removal.
